In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of sediment in controlling the slope of bedrock channels, and the implications of the threshold of motion and other sediment-related effects on the behavior of bedrock channel incision models.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sediment transport and bedrock erosion by sediment abrasion are both important in bedrock river incision, but that the threshold of grain movement, the cover effect, and the tools effect are more important than the threshold of suspension in controlling the steady-state channel profile slope, and that the effect of sediment on bed incision can be represented with a reasonable degree of accuracy using the saltation– abrasion model.

the threshold of grain movement is the most important sediment effect that should be accounted for in models of bedrock channel slope, followed in order by the cover effect and the tools effect, and that models should be developed with the understanding that sediment supply and transport are likely to be the most important controls of channel slope.

the threshold of grain movement is the single most important effect of sediment on bed incision that must be represented explicitly in order to predict the steady-state channel gradient, and that the saltation–abrasion model provides a useful reference for evaluating the performance of alternative incision model formulations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the saltation–abrsion model predicts that the steady-state channel gradient is a sensitive function of the size distribution of sediment delivered by hillslopes, which is determined by the rock uplift rate, the rock strength, and the hillslope processes that transport sediment.

the saltation–abrsion incision model is an important reference for evaluating alternative incision models in terms of their ability to predict steady-state channel slope, and that the saltation-abrsion model is a good starting point for developing new incision models.
the saltation– abrasion model is an important step towards the development of a mechanistic, quantitative, and process-based model for predicting topographic slope.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the saltation-abrsion model, which is the most complete of the models considered, predicts that channel slope depends primarily on grain size, and that rock uplift rate and strength have only a secondary effect on slope, through their influence on grain size.
the threshold of grain mobility is the key sediment effect on channel incision, and that the threshold of mobility should be represented explicitly in incision models.

the saltation– abrasion model provides a useful reference for evaluating the predictions of alternative bedrock incision models, and the implications of those models for predicting the topographic steady-state slope of bedrock river channels.
